To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

carcinoma cells are characterized by the presence of cytoplasmic projections, enlarged mitochondria, and an absence of glycogen; that carcinoma in situ is distinguished from invasive carcinoma by the presence of a basement membrane; and that invasive carcinoma is characterized by the absence of a basement membrane.
the nuclei of malignant tumor cell reveal the following notable alteration: increased nuclear membrane foldings, increased density chromatin granules, and enlargement of the nucleolus.

carcinoma in situ cells have more nuclear infoldings and more glycogen than normal cervical epithelum cells, while invasive carcinoma cells have more mitochondria and fewer attachment plates than normal cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the ultrastructure of the cervical epithelium in the normal, in carcinoma in situ of the cervix, and in invasive carcinoma of the same tissue.
the ultrastructural study of the normal cervical epithelum and of carcinoma in situ.

the electron microscopic study of the ultrastructural changes in carcinoma cells in the uterine cervix, with particular reference to the relationship between carcinoma in situ and the invasive carcinoma.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
carcinoma in situ is a true neoplastic process with a definite malignant potential, but that the neoplasm is still confined within the basement membrane and has not invaded the underlying stroma.

the ultrastructural characteristics of carcinoma in situ are similar to those of normal cervical epithelum except for the following differences: 1) increased infoldings of the nuclear membrane; 2) enlargement of the nucleoli with more pronounced differentiation between dense and granular areas; 3) occasional droplets of glycogen in the cytoplam; 4) presence of villous projections at the cell membrane; and 5) absence of the dense plaque at the cell membrane.
, in carcinoma of the cervic, there are definite ultrastructural alterations of the nuclei and cytoplasm of malignant cells as compared with normal cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the most prominent ultrastructural changes in the nuclei and cytoplasm of malignant cells are the increased number of mitochondria, the absence of glycogen, the absence of the dense cytoplasm plaques at the attachment plates, and the presence of villous cytoplasmic processes at the cell surface.
the ultrastructural changes in carcinoma cells are more pronounced in invasive carcinoma than carcinoma in situ.

carcinoma in situ and the invasive carcinoma of the uterine cervix show a number of ultrastructural changes, which may be considered as the morphologic expression of malignancy in the cervical epithelium.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the basement membrane is not a reliable criterion for differentiating carcinoma in situ from invasive carcinoma of the uterine cervix.
the ultrastructure of invasive carcinoma cells shows a more marked deviation from normal than that of carcinoma in situ.
electron microscopic examination of cervical carcinoma in situ and of invasive carcinoma of the uterus can provide useful information in the evaluation of these lesions.
